articles.title: Google Photos users report handy drag-to-select feature has disappeared
articles.summary: Credit: Taylor Kerns / Android Authority TL;DR Google Photos users are reporting that a feature has suddenly gone missing. The affected users can no longer drag to select multiple photos. This problem has been spotted on Pixel, Galaxy, and OnePlus phones. Recently, Google Photos users have noticed that the app won’t let them search for terms related to regulated or illicit substances . While that appears to be an intentional choice implemented into Google’s guardrails, a new issue has popped up that seems unintentional. A convenient photo selection feature has suddenly disappeared from the app for some. Google Photos users are flocking to Reddit to report that drag to select no longer works for them. If you’re unfamiliar with drag to select, the feature allows you to select multiple photos

articles.title: Weekly poll results: smart glasses are a solution looking for a problem
articles.summary: Tech giants are spending tons of R&D money on building new smart glasses that fill various categories. However, based on the results from last week’s poll, all of them are solutions looking for a problem. The outcome couldn’t be more clear – the vast majority of voters are not using smart glasses. To be fair, regional availability is preventing some people from trying them out. But even then it’s clear that most people haven’t found a compelling use-case for them. articles.title: AI adoption isn’t the same as AI usage
articles.summary: Every engineering org I’ve talked to this year has some version of the same chart. Seat activations climbing. Token spend climbing. Somebody’s slide says 80% weekly active. Then you sit in that team’s planning meeting, and nothing about how they build software has changed. That gap is the actual problem, and most of the way we measure AI adoption is designed, accidentally, to hide it. Everything you’re measuring is a usage metric Token spend tells you someone typed into a box. Pull request count tells you commits landed. “Percentage of code written by AI” tells you an autocomplete got accepted. None of it tells you the work got better. Goodhart’s Law, right on schedule.
